t.1.83.1: Indra said: Having completed all your works, O king, and having abandoned your home, you went to the forest. So I ask you, son of Nahuṣa: to whom are you equal in austerity, O Yayāti?
t.1.83.2: Yayāti said: Among gods and men, among Gandharvas and great seers, I see no one equal to myself in austerity, O Vāsava.
t.1.83.4: Yayāti said: If, O Śakra, my worlds have come to destruction because of my contempt for gods, seers, Gandharvas and men, then, deprived of the world of the gods, I would wish to fall among the good, O king of the gods.
t.1.83.3: Because you, ignorant of their power, have looked down on your equals, your betters and your inferiors alike, these worlds of yours have an end; your merit exhausted, you will fall today, O king.
t.1.83.6: Then, seeing Yayāti falling, having left the holy worlds frequented by the king of the immortals, Aṣṭaka, best of royal seers and guardian of the ordinances of true dharma, spoke to him.
t.1.83.5: You will fall, O king, into the presence of the good, and though fallen, you will there once more gain a firm footing. Knowing this, Yayāti, never again should your equals and your betters be disdained by you.
t.1.83.7: Who are you, a youth whose form is like that of Vāsava, blazing with your own splendor like fire, falling from the sky out of the darkness of the risen rain-clouds like the sun, foremost of those that move through the heavens?
t.1.83.8: And seeing you falling from the path of the sun, immeasurable, with the radiance of Vaiśvānara and the sun, we were all bewildered, wondering, "What can this be that is falling?"
t.1.83.9: Seeing you standing on the path of the gods, you whose might is like that of Śakra, the Sun, and Viṣṇu, we have all come forth today to meet you, wishing to know the truth about your fall.
t.1.83.10: We did not dare to question you first, nor do you ask us who we are. So we ask you, whose form is so enviable: whose son are you, and for what reason have you come?
t.1.83.11: Let your fear depart, and quickly cast off despair and delusion, O you whose form is like that of the lord of the gods; for while you abide in the presence of the good, not even Śakra, the slayer of Bala, is able to overpower you.
t.1.83.12: For the good are ever the refuge of the good who have fallen from happiness, O you who are like the king of the immortals. These lords of all that is stationary and moving are gathered here; you are established among the good, who are your equals.
t.1.83.13: Fire is master in burning, the earth is master in the sowing of seed, the sun is master in giving light, and among the good, the guest who has arrived is master.
